point_one.role: Add a mechanistic nuance to the circadian explanation: a regular sleep–wake schedule can act as a weak time cue, but the internal pacemaker has limits on what schedules it can follow. This makes the body’s timing system look like a stabilizer rather than a perfectly calibrated alarm.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: In the laboratory, weak light plus a scheduled routine entrained people to a 24.0-hour day, but generally not to 23.5- or 24.6-hour cycles. The specific insight is that regular mornings may strengthen timing near the body’s natural near-24-hour rhythm without giving it unlimited precision.
point_one.evidence_anchor: F001 shows entrainment at 24.0 hours but not usually at 23.5 or 24.6 hours; F016 establishes light as a major environmental cue for circadian phase-setting.
point_one.why_it_matters: This explains why waking before an alarm may become more plausible when someone follows a stable schedule, while irregular routines or schedules misaligned with the internal clock are less likely to produce reliable pre-alarm waking. The routine helps organize the timing system, but it does not make the body an exact countdown timer.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the basic claim that light and regular sleep–wake timing synchronize the circadian clock, or re-explain the headline evidence that physiological changes begin before waking. The point should focus specifically on the 24.0-versus-23.5/24.6-hour entrainment boundary.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss deliberate self-awakening, practice effects, reported success rates, or the distinction between a habitual skill and an accidental awakening before an alarm. Those belong to Point Two.

point_two.role: Reframe self-awakening as a possible expectation-and-practice phenomenon, not merely as evidence of a biological clock predicting an alarm. The point should use contrasting behavioral data to show that planned waking can improve with repetition but is not a uniform human trait.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: Among 11 people without a self-awakening habit, 82% succeeded on the seventh day of repeated alarm-free attempts, whereas only 10.3% of 643 university students reported routinely self-awakening. The new perspective is that occasional success, a learned routine, and a broadly reliable ability are three different claims.
point_two.evidence_anchor: F007 reports 82% success on day seven after a week of practice; F004 reports a 10.3% self-reported habitual rate; F003 and F017 document the varied definitions and procedures across 17 studies involving 715 participants.
point_two.why_it_matters: For listeners, repeatedly waking near a target time may reflect the interaction of expectation, rehearsal, and regular sleep timing rather than proof that the body can precisely foresee an alarm. This also suggests why the experience can feel dependable for some people yet fail or remain uncommon for others.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the core pre-awakening ACTH, brain-activity, or heart-rate findings, and do not use the point only to restate that existing studies do not directly test accidental waking immediately before an alarm. That distinction should appear only as a brief qualification to the practice-and-expectation insight.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss light, the SCN, the 24.0-versus-23.5/24.6-hour entrainment limit, or the circadian system’s general synchronization mechanism. Those are Point One’s focus.
